oe.title: Volumetric analysis procedures
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Standard solution: weigh solute accurately, dissolve in a beaker of deionised water, transfer with rinsings to a volumetric flask, make up to the mark (bottom of meniscus at eye level) and invert to mix.
Pipette: rinse with the solution to be measured, fill with a pipette filler to above the mark and adjust so the bottom of the meniscus is on the line; transfer to a conical flask.
Burette: rinse with the titrant, fill (remove the air bubble from the tip), and read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Add an indicator (or use a self-indicating reagent such as permanganate). Place a white tile under the flask, swirl, and add dropwise near the end-point.
Do a rough titration first, then repeat until concordant titres (within 0·1 or 0·2 cm³); average the concordant results.
Calculation: moles = c × V (in litres); use the mole ratio from the balanced equation; c = n ÷ V.
Equations, calculations and diagrams to consider
Example equation with mole ratio, e.g. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, or a redox example such as MnO₄⁻ with Fe²⁺ (1 : 5).
Worked example: concordant titre → moles of titrant → moles of analyte → concentration.
Labelled diagram of titration apparatus (burette, clamp, conical flask, white tile).

r.label: Question 9

oe.title: Seabirds and oil spills
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Crude oil is mainly non-polar hydrocarbons, insoluble in water (cannot hydrogen bond), so it floats and coats feathers.
Oil disrupts the structure that traps air, so feathers lose waterproofing and insulation (hypothermia) and buoyancy.
Vegetable oil is also non-polar, so it dissolves and loosens the crude oil (like dissolves like) without harming the bird. It is non-toxic if swallowed.
Washing-up liquid (detergent): the hydrophobic tail dissolves in the oil and the hydrophilic head dissolves in water, forming droplets (an emulsion) that rinse away.
Dilute detergent is used because concentrated detergent could strip natural oils from feathers or irritate skin.
Swallowed hydrocarbons are non-polar and can dissolve in fatty tissues, damaging organs.
Diagrams to consider
Detergent molecule (labelled hydrophobic tail and hydrophilic head) and an oil droplet surrounded by detergent molecules with heads pointing into the water.
Diagram contrasting the London forces between hydrocarbon molecules with the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.

r.txt:

This causes problems for birds because their feathers lose their waterproofing, making the birds susceptible to temperature changes and affecting their buoyancy. If the birds attempt to clean themselves to remove the oil, they may swallow the hydrocarbons causing damage to their internal organs.

Contaminated seabirds can be cleaned by rubbing vegetable oil into their feathers and feet before the birds are rinsed with diluted washing-up liquid.
